w: Built from 1079 to 1532, dedicated to St Swithun, this is the longest medieval cathedral in the world at 558 feet, with a vast Perpendicular nave, Norman transepts and tower, and an Early English retroquire. It draws over 350,000 visitors a year and ranks sixth-largest UK cathedral by area.
s: The longest medieval cathedral in the world

w: Founded in 1067 by William the Conqueror as a royal seat, little survives but the Great Hall - one of England's finest medieval halls, now a museum - and the Westgate, its old defensive gateway. The Great Hall holds the famous Round Table, a giant oak tabletop linked to the Arthurian legend since medieval times.
s: Home to the Great Hall's Arthurian Round Table

w: The ruined medieval palace of the Bishops of Winchester, built mostly by Henry of Blois in the 12th century. Fortified during the civil-war chaos of the Anarchy, it was more residence than fortress. Only its 15th-century chapel survives intact, folded into the bishop's current home, Wolvesey Palace, next door.

w: Winchester's Anglo-Saxon cathedral, standing immediately north of, and partly beneath, its successor from 660 until 1093. St Swithun was buried here in 862; by the 10th century it was rebuilt on a vast scale, briefly the largest church in Europe, its bells said to ring hopelessly tangled with the New Minster next door.

w: Christopher Wren's abandoned palace for Charles II, begun in 1683 and modelled on Versailles. Wren promised it in a year; Charles died before it was finished. Gutted by fire in 1894, its salvaged masonry was built into the Peninsula Barracks, which now house Winchester's Military Museums.
